MLP vs SVM: should VTSearch swap the model that learns your search?

VTSearch learns what you're looking for from a handful of good/bad votes and ranks the rest of your collection. Today a tiny neural network (an MLP) does that learning. Would a classic Support Vector Machine rank better — and if so, which kind?

2026-07-22 · HLTCOE grid · branch claude/mlp-vs-svm-experiment · PR #2683 · raw data + markdown in docs/experiments/mlp-vs-svm/

3image datasets · SigLIP 768-d
150voting trajectories (5 cats × 2 arms × 5 seeds)
≤200votes simulated per run
3rankers: MLP, linear-SVM, RBF-SVM
Keepthe MLP — verdict

Verdict: keep the MLP. The result is not a blowout — it's a crossover. The SVMs are more accurate for the first ~50 votes (they make fewer mistakes when trained on just a handful of clean examples), but the MLP overtakes them by ~vote 100 and wins decisively by 200, and it misses fewer matches in the rare-event case VTSearch is built for. Under the pre-registered rule, no SVM variant qualified to replace the MLP.

Take-aways

The SVMs win the first few dozen votes; the MLP wins the session. Averaged across datasets, the SVMs reach a lower cost than the MLP by vote 50 (MLP 0.387 vs linear 0.331, RBF 0.330), but the MLP keeps improving as votes accumulate and is already ahead by vote 100 (0.359 vs 0.378 / 0.390), pulling clear by vote 200 (0.286 vs 0.373 / 0.402). This is the textbook trade-off: the SVM's margin-based fit is very label-efficient on a few clean votes; the MLP's "every example is evidence" learning compounds as evidence grows.

On rare (1%-prevalence) events, the MLP misses fewer real matches. At vote 50 in the rare arm the MLP's miss rate (FNR) is 0.285, well below the SVMs' (~0.41). Rare-event search is VTSearch's headline use case, so this is the decisive column — a model that trades misses for fewer false alarms at 1% prevalence loses even when total cost ties.

"Win early" means accuracy, not speed. Cost here is error rate (false alarms + misses) on held-out data, not runtime. At the vote counts users actually reach, both models fit and score in milliseconds — speed is a tiebreaker, not a driver.

For product decisions: keep the MLP as the default ranker. A hybrid (SVM for the first ~40–60 votes, then the MLP) is a plausible way to grab the early edge, but the gain is small and brief and a mid-session model switch risks a threshold discontinuity and worse rare-event recall — it's documented as a testable follow-up, not a recommendation.

What we measured, in plain terms

Three candidate rankers, each with a different idea of what your votes mean:

MLP treats every vote as evidence about a probability; a stray bad vote gets outvoted by the bulk, and it can carve out a concept made of several separate clusters. Linear SVM draws the single straightest dividing line between good and bad, fixed by the hardest few examples near the boundary — very label-efficient when votes are clean, but one mis-vote near the line can distort it. RBF (kernel) SVM draws a curved, local boundary; far from anything it has seen it defaults to "not the thing" — cautious, which can suppress false alarms in unexplored corners but can also miss genuinely new pockets of matches.

Crucially, we measured each the way you actually experience VTSearch: votes are cast in the order the app's Autopilot presents them (seeded by a text search, then good/bad/refine/explore phases), the production threshold-picking path runs unchanged, and every error is counted on a held-out half of the data the model never votes on.

How to read the charts. FPR (false-positive rate) is the fraction of non-matches wrongly flagged — false alarms; lower is better. FNR (false-negative rate) is the fraction of real matches missed; lower is better. Cost = FPR + FNR is total error; lower is better. The x-axis is votes cast, so a curve that drops lower with fewer votes is a better ranker. The natural row is each category's real rarity; the rare row thins matches to 1% to stress-test rare-event search.

The crossover, in numbers

Mean cost across categories × seeds at fixed vote counts (lower is better). The winner flips between vote 50 and vote 100:

t = 250.3990.3280.333SVM

t = 1000.3590.3780.390MLP
t = 2000.2860.3730.402MLP
rare FNR @ t=500.2850.4120.404MLP

Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank (Holm-corrected) confirms both ends are real, not noise: the SVMs beat the MLP at t=50 (p = 0.025 / 0.014) and the MLP beats the SVMs at t=200 (p < 0.001 for both). Over the whole session (area under the cost curve) the difference is not significant (p = 0.83 / 0.16) — they roughly tie on average, but the pre-registered rule requires winning at both 50 and 200 votes without giving up rare-event recall, which no SVM does.

Which SVM, and how fast?

A cheap screen first picked the best configuration of each SVM kernel family (linear, RBF, polynomial, sigmoid) before the head-to-head; the definitive run then compared the MLP against the two strongest (linear and RBF).

Runtime was measured as a tiebreaker only. Note: the cluster's GPU SVM library (cuML) is installed but its kernels fail to compile here (a CUDA-toolchain mismatch), so the SVMs ran on the CPU while the MLP ran on the GPU — the report compares MLP-GPU vs SVM-CPU and the shape of the scaling is what matters, not the absolute crossover.

MLP (torch, GPU) linear-SVM (sklearn, CPU) RBF-SVM (sklearn, CPU)

Honest caveats

Closed-loop by design. Autopilot picks the next vote from the current model's scores, so the MLP and SVM trajectories diverge after the first retrain even at the same seed. That's intentional — the question is which model makes VTSearch better — but it means we compared whole systems, not models on identical vote sequences.

Calibration asymmetry. The MLP uses production's exact threshold calibration; the SVMs use the natural trainer-agnostic analogue. A small source of unfairness, accepted so the MLP path reproduces production byte-for-byte.

Scope. Image + SigLIP only, and — because the cluster throttled GPU concurrency — a balanced 5-category × 5-seed grid rather than the full 8×10. The datasets are caltech101_m (objects), visual_genome_m (multi-label "does X appear"), and vggface2_faces_m (identity). Findings may not transfer to audio, video, text, or region embedders — the harness is built to test those next.
